prerequisites: Organisms may consist of one cell or many cells.
goals: Explain the shared life processes in context.
Distinguish respiration from breathing and excretion from egestion.
Compare plants, animals, fungi and protoctists using several features.
Distinguish bacterial cells from viruses and explain what makes a pathogen.

sections.title: Shared characteristics of living organisms
paragraphs: Living organisms obtain materials and energy, respond to change, and maintain themselves. Nutrition provides materials for growth and the chemical reactions that sustain life. Respiration transfers energy through reactions inside cells; it is not defined by whether an organism has lungs.

Excretion removes waste products of metabolism, such as carbon dioxide produced in respiration. Egestion removes undigested material from the digestive system. The source of the waste matters: not every material leaving an organism is a metabolic waste product.

Organisms respond to their surroundings and show movement. Movement need not mean travelling from place to place: a plant shoot can grow towards light. They control internal conditions, reproduce, and grow and develop. Internal control is called homeostasis; it helps keep conditions suitable for cells despite external change.

Use the characteristics together. A moving object is not necessarily alive, and a dormant seed is not necessarily dead. Reproduction is a characteristic of living organisms across generations; an individual’s inability to reproduce does not by itself make that individual non-living.

example.question: A germinating seed releases carbon dioxide and its root grows downwards. Which life processes do these observations support?
steps: Carbon dioxide is consistent with respiration taking place in the seed’s cells.
Release of a metabolic waste product illustrates excretion.
Root growth illustrates growth and movement, while its direction shows a response to the surroundings.
example.explanation: Each observation is linked to a named process. No claim is made that these observations alone demonstrate every characteristic of life.

practice.question: Explain why a plant can respire even though it has no lungs.
practice.answer: Respiration is a set of chemical reactions in cells that transfers energy. Lungs are organs for gas exchange in some animals, not a requirement for respiration.
practice.explanation: The key distinction is between a cellular process and one animal structure that supplies gases.

sections.title: Plants and animals: compare the evidence
paragraphs: Eukaryotes have cells with genetic material enclosed in a nucleus. Plants and animals are multicellular eukaryotes. Classification uses a combination of features; being green or being able to move is not enough on its own.

Plant cells have walls made of cellulose. Photosynthetic plant cells contain chloroplasts, where light energy is used to make organic food. Plants store carbohydrate as starch and can also store it as sucrose. Not every plant cell contains chloroplasts: underground root cells usually do not.

Animals have no cell walls or chloroplasts and do not photosynthesise. They obtain organic food by feeding on other organisms or their products. Most have nervous coordination and can move from place to place; glycogen is an important carbohydrate store.

Maize is a flowering cereal plant; peas and beans are herbaceous legumes. Humans are mammals, whereas houseflies and mosquitoes are insects. These are examples within the plant and animal groups, not definitions of those groups.

example.question: An organism has many cells, cellulose cell walls and chloroplasts in its leaf cells. Explain its likely group.
steps: Many cells are consistent with either a plant or an animal.
Cellulose walls and chloroplasts support classification as a plant.
Use the combination, rather than multicellularity alone.
example.explanation: Each stated observation is linked to a distinguishing feature.

practice.question: A root cell has no chloroplasts. Does that make the organism an animal?
practice.answer: No. Specialised root cells usually lack chloroplasts. Other evidence, including cellulose cell walls and the whole organism, is needed.
practice.explanation: A feature of one specialised cell need not describe every cell of an organism.

commonMistakes: Do not say every plant cell has chloroplasts.
Both plants and animals respire; photosynthesis does not replace respiration.

sections.title: Fungi and feeding outside the body
paragraphs: Fungi are eukaryotes that do not photosynthesise. Their cell walls contain chitin rather than cellulose. They may store carbohydrate as glycogen, so a carbohydrate store alone cannot distinguish fungi from animals.

Many fungi grow as branching threads called hyphae. A network of hyphae forms a mycelium, and the hyphae contain many nuclei. Mucor illustrates this form. Yeast is a single-celled fungus, so being multicellular is not a requirement for membership of the fungal group.

In saprotrophic nutrition, a fungus releases digestive enzymes onto dead organic material. Digestion happens outside the organism: large insoluble food molecules are broken into smaller soluble products, which the fungus absorbs. Enzyme secretion and absorption are different steps. Not every fungus is a harmless decomposer; some fungi are pathogens.

example.question: Explain how a fungus can obtain nutrients from a piece of dead plant material without swallowing it.
steps: Digestive enzymes are secreted onto the material.
The enzymes break large food molecules into soluble products outside the fungus.
The products are absorbed by the fungus.
example.explanation: The location of digestion and the direction of absorption both matter.

practice.question: Give two features that distinguish a fungus from a plant.
practice.answer: Fungi lack chloroplasts and do not photosynthesise; fungal cell walls contain chitin rather than cellulose.
practice.explanation: Compare the same feature in both groups, rather than listing unrelated facts.

commonMistakes: Digestive enzymes are secreted; the digested products are absorbed.
Yeast is a fungus despite being single-celled.

sections.title: Protoctists: similar cells, different ways of life
paragraphs: The protoctist examples in this syllabus are microscopic, single-celled eukaryotes. They have nuclei, unlike bacteria. Their other features vary, so do not assume that all protoctists have chloroplasts or cause disease.

Amoeba, found in pond water, has animal-like cell features and obtains food rather than photosynthesising. Chlorella contains chloroplasts and photosynthesises. Plasmodium is a pathogenic protoctist that causes malaria. A mosquito can transmit the parasite, but the mosquito and the pathogen are different organisms.

example.question: A microscopic organism consists of one cell with a nucleus and chloroplasts. Which syllabus example fits?
steps: A nucleus supports a eukaryotic cell rather than a bacterium.
A single cell with chloroplasts fits Chlorella, a protoctist.
Chloroplasts alone do not show that the organism is a multicellular plant.
example.explanation: The combination of cellular organisation and structures is more useful than one feature.

practice.question: Why is Plasmodium described as both a protoctist and a pathogen?
practice.answer: Protoctist describes its organism group; pathogen describes its ability to cause disease, in this case malaria.
practice.explanation: The terms answer different questions and are not competing classifications.

commonMistakes: A mosquito transmits the malaria pathogen; it is not Plasmodium.
Do not give every protoctist the features of Chlorella.

sections.title: Bacteria: cells without a nucleus
paragraphs: Bacteria are microscopic, single-celled prokaryotes. They have a cell membrane surrounding cytoplasm and a cell wall outside the membrane. Their main DNA is a circular chromosome in the cytoplasm, not enclosed in a nucleus.

Plasmids are small additional circular DNA molecules; they are separate from the main chromosome. The specification includes plasmids among bacterial features. Distinguish this typical bacterial model from a claim that every individual bacterium must carry plasmids.

Some bacteria photosynthesise, but most obtain nutrients from living organisms or dead organic material. Their cell walls are not the cellulose walls of plants. Having a cell wall therefore does not by itself identify a cell as a plant.

Lactobacillus bulgaricus is a rod-shaped bacterium used when producing yoghurt from milk. Pneumococcus is a spherical bacterium that can cause pneumonia. These examples show why it is incorrect to label all bacteria harmful.

example.question: A diagram shows a small cell with cytoplasm, a cell wall, a circular chromosome and two plasmids, but no nucleus. Explain its classification.
steps: The lack of a nucleus and a circular chromosome fit a prokaryotic cell.
The wall, membrane and cytoplasm are consistent with a bacterium.
The plasmids are additional DNA loops, not nuclei.
example.explanation: The absence of a nucleus does not mean the absence of genetic material.

practice.question: Compare the genetic material in a typical bacterial cell and a typical animal cell.
practice.answer: A bacterium has a circular chromosome not enclosed by a nucleus and may contain plasmids. An animal cell normally has its chromosomes inside a nucleus.
practice.explanation: Name both the DNA arrangement and its location; do not say bacteria have no DNA.

commonMistakes: No nucleus does not mean no DNA.
Bacteria are cells; viruses are not cells.

sections.title: Pathogens and hosts
paragraphs: A pathogen is a disease-causing agent. Pathogens can be fungi, bacteria, protoctists or viruses. The name describes their effect on a host; it does not mean that every member of any one group causes disease.

A host is an organism in or on which another agent lives or reproduces. Match the pathogen to its group and disease: Plasmodium is a protoctist causing malaria, whereas Pneumococcus is a bacterium that can cause pneumonia. Useful bacteria and non-pathogenic fungi still belong to their respective groups.

When explaining evidence, separate a symptom, a disease and its cause. A visible change in an organism is an observation; identifying the responsible pathogen requires more information than that observation alone.

example.question: A student says that any microscopic organism found on food is a pathogen. Evaluate this claim.
steps: A pathogen must be capable of causing disease.
Microscopic size alone does not establish that property.
Some microorganisms are useful, such as bacteria used in yoghurt production.
example.explanation: Challenge the proposed rule using the definition and a relevant counterexample.

practice.question: Name four groups that can contain pathogens.
practice.explanation: Viruses can be pathogens even though they are not classified as living organisms in this syllabus.

commonMistakes: Pathogen is not a synonym for bacterium.
Not every microorganism is a pathogen.

sections.title: Viruses: reproduction depends on living cells
paragraphs: Viruses are non-cellular particles and are not classified as living organisms in this syllabus. They are smaller than bacteria. Their genetic material is enclosed in a protein coat; a virus contains DNA or RNA as its genetic material, rather than both types as its genome. Viruses have varied shapes and sizes.

Viruses reproduce only inside living host cells, using the host cell’s machinery to make new virus particles. They do not have their own cellular organisation, cytoplasm or independent metabolism. Reproduction inside a host does not demonstrate that a free virus particle carries out all the characteristics of life.

Viruses infect all major groups of living organisms, including plants, animals and bacteria, but a particular virus has a limited host range. Tobacco mosaic virus affects tobacco plants, disrupting chloroplast formation and producing discoloured leaves. Influenza virus causes flu. HIV can cause AIDS by damaging the immune system; HIV is the virus and AIDS is the resulting syndrome, not a second virus.

example.question: Why is the observation that viruses reproduce not enough to classify them as living organisms in this course?
steps: They reproduce only inside living host cells.
They are not made of cells and lack independent metabolism.
The characteristics of life must be considered together.
example.explanation: A single property is not a complete classification test.

practice.question: State two differences between a bacterium and a virus.
practice.answer: A bacterium is a cell with cytoplasm and a membrane; a virus is non-cellular with genetic material in a protein coat. A virus needs living host cells to reproduce, whereas bacteria reproduce as cells.
practice.explanation: Pair each difference directly. Do not claim that bacteria lack genetic material.

commonMistakes: A virus is not a small bacterial cell.
Viruses can infect plants as well as animals.

sections.title: Build a classification argument
paragraphs: Begin with the strongest structural evidence. A nucleus supports eukaryotic organisation; a cell with a circular chromosome and no nucleus supports prokaryotic organisation. A protein coat surrounding genetic material without cellular structures supports a virus. Then use nutrition, cell-wall material and number of cells to distinguish the eukaryotic groups.

Use paired comparisons: plant cellulose walls versus fungal chitin walls; photosynthesis in Chlorella versus feeding in Amoeba; a bacterial chromosome in cytoplasm versus chromosomes enclosed in a eukaryotic nucleus. State only what the observations support. A cell wall, a green colour or the ability to move is rarely a sufficient argument alone.

example.question: An unfamiliar organism has chitin cell walls, many branching threads and no chloroplasts. Identify its group and justify your answer.
steps: Chitin walls are characteristic of fungi.
The threads fit hyphae forming a mycelium.
Lack of chloroplasts is consistent with a fungus that does not photosynthesise.
example.explanation: Three linked observations make the conclusion stronger than simply stating that it is not green.

practice.question: A specimen has a cell wall. Can you decide whether it is a plant, fungus or bacterium?
practice.answer: No. All three can have cell walls. Evidence about wall material, the nucleus, chloroplasts or overall organisation is needed.
practice.explanation: Explain the limitation, then identify what extra information would resolve it.

commonMistakes: Give a reason for the classification, not just a group name.
Do not infer a nucleus merely from the presence of DNA.

sections.title: Explain observations without inventing missing evidence
paragraphs: Nutrition supplies materials and an energy source for the reactions of life. A green plant absorbs water and mineral ions and makes organic food by photosynthesis; light supplies the energy for that synthesis. An animal takes in organic food and digests and absorbs suitable molecules. Soil minerals are not the plant’s main source of energy, and photosynthesis does not replace respiration.

Cellular respiration transfers energy from organic molecules. Plant cells and germinating seeds respire without lungs. Gas exchange supplies or removes gases; breathing moves air in and out of an animal’s lungs. These are related processes, not three names for the same process.

Excretion removes waste from metabolic reactions. Carbon dioxide made in respiration and urea made from excess amino acids are examples. Undigested fibre leaving the gut is egested: it did not become waste through a cellular reaction. Identify the origin of a substance, not simply the exit it uses.

The observations below are invented classroom cases, not results of an experiment. A single observation can support several characteristics, but cannot establish every characteristic or the exact mechanism by itself.

rows: A leaf produces organic food in light; an animal absorbs digested food.
Contrasting ways of obtaining organic nutrients.
This does not mean a plant obtains energy by eating soil minerals.
A germinating seed takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide in darkness.
Consistent with aerobic respiration and removal of metabolic carbon dioxide.
No lungs or photosynthesis are required for this observation.
An animal passes undigested fibre and releases carbon dioxide made in its cells.
Egestion of fibre; excretion of metabolic carbon dioxide.
Material leaving the body is not automatically an excretory product.

example.question: An investigator says that a dark-grown seed cannot respire because it has no lungs and cannot photosynthesise. Correct both parts of the reasoning.
steps: Respiration transfers energy through reactions in the seed’s cells, not in lungs.
The seed can use stored organic food; photosynthesis is not required for these respiration reactions.
Darkness therefore does not establish absence of respiration.
example.explanation: The answer distinguishes a cellular energy-transfer process from photosynthetic food synthesis and animal ventilation.

practice.question: In invented cases, a green plant makes organic food and an animal absorbs digested food. The animal also passes undigested fibre and excretes urea produced from excess amino acids. Explain the nutrition comparison and classify both outgoing materials.
practice.answer: The plant makes organic food by photosynthesis, using light energy, whereas the animal obtains organic nutrients from its food. Fibre is egested because it remains undigested. Urea is excreted because it is a waste product of metabolism.
practice.explanation: Judge food acquisition and waste origin separately; neither soil minerals nor the removal of any material alone defines the required process.

sections.title: Movement, responses and internal regulation
paragraphs: A change in the surroundings is a stimulus; the resulting change in an organism is a response. A rooted shoot bending towards a lamp shows directional growth and movement without locomotion of the whole plant. Its direction is evidence of a response to light. Movement and response can overlap, but an organism does not have to travel from place to place.

Homeostasis means regulating internal conditions so cells can function despite external changes. It is active regulation within suitable ranges, not an assertion that every internal measurement is exactly constant. External temperature and internal body temperature are different variables.

Invented mammal measurements are 37.0°C internally in air at 20°C and 37.1°C internally in air at 30°C. They are consistent with internal temperature regulation. Two measurements alone do not identify the mechanism or prove regulation of glucose, water or every other internal condition.

example.question: A plant remains rooted while its shoot bends towards a lamp. Name two characteristics supported by the observation and explain why locomotion is unnecessary.
steps: The position or shape of part of the plant changes, so it shows movement.
The direction changes in relation to light, supporting response to the surroundings.
Movement of a part can occur without the whole organism changing location.
example.explanation: The response is linked to a particular stimulus; being rooted does not rule out movement.

practice.question: Invented readings show air temperature changing from 18°C to 29°C while a mammal’s internal temperature changes from 36.9°C to 37.1°C. A rooted seedling also bends towards a window. What characteristic does each case support, and what stronger claims would be unjustified?
practice.answer: The mammal readings are consistent with regulation of internal temperature despite an external change; they do not prove an exactly constant temperature, its mechanism or control of every internal variable. The seedling shows movement and a response to light while remaining rooted; it need not travel from place to place.
practice.explanation: Each claim stays within its evidence and distinguishes internal regulation from simply matching the surroundings.

sections.title: Growth and development are not reproduction
paragraphs: Growth is a lasting increase in size or mass, usually involving increases in cell number or cell size. Development involves changes in structure and function, such as formation and differentiation of leaves in a seedling. A shoot getting longer supports growth; the appearance of functioning new organs supports development. A short-term change in water content alone is not sufficient proof of biological growth.

Reproduction produces new individuals and maintains a lineage across generations. The growth of one individual is not reproduction. A flowering plant producing viable seeds that develop into offspring illustrates reproduction; a shoot merely increasing in height does not establish it.

Not every living individual reproduces at every moment or is capable of doing so. Juvenile and infertile individuals can still be alive. The shared characteristic describes organisms and their lineages, rather than a compulsory event that every individual must display during one observation.

A wind-up toy moves; a balloon becomes larger when inflated. These changes do not demonstrate cellular nutrition, respiration, metabolic excretion or controlled biological development. Use converging evidence across the characteristics instead of treating one resemblance as a test of life.

example.question: In invented observations, a seedling’s dry mass increases and new leaves form. Later the mature plant produces viable seeds that become new plants. Distinguish growth, development and reproduction.
steps: The increase in dry mass supports growth rather than a temporary water-only change.
New leaf structure and function support development.
Viable seeds developing into new individuals support reproduction, separate from the first plant becoming larger.
example.explanation: The answer relates each observation to its own process rather than assigning all changes to reproduction.

practice.question: A young organism grows and develops but has not reproduced. A wind-up toy moves when wound. Explain why neither observation justifies declaring the young organism non-living or the toy living.
practice.answer: Reproduction is a lineage characteristic and is not required to occur in every individual or during a short observation; a juvenile can be alive. The toy’s movement alone does not establish cellular nutrition, respiration, excretion, regulation, biological growth/development or reproduction. Several relevant characteristics and cellular evidence must be considered together.
practice.explanation: The comparison distinguishes an absence of current reproductive activity from evidence of non-life, and avoids a one-feature classification rule.
